text: Through love, bitter turns sweet and *copper turns to gold*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book II, story of Luqman (Ganjoor II §31, couplet 20; c. II.1529–30 in Nicholson)
original: از محبت تلخ‌ها شیرین شود / از محبت مس‌ها زرین شود

text: Lord, if I worship you from fear of hell, burn me in it; if from hope of paradise, deny it to me. If I worship you *for your own sake*, do not hide your lasting beauty from me.
author: Rabia al-Adawiyya
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Rabia
original: خداوندا اگر تو را از بیم دوزخ می‌پرستم در دوزخم بسوز و اگر به امید بهشت می‌پرستم بر من حرام گردان و اگر برای تو تو را می‌پرستم جمال باقی دریغ مدار
note: Attar wrote this down in Persian about four centuries after Rabia. Nothing in her own hand survives.

text: I did not come to quarrel; my work is love. The Friend lives in hearts, and I came *to build hearts*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem with the couplet “Ben gelmedim dava için” (Tatcı ed., poem 179, couplet 2)
original: Ben gelmedim dava için, benim işim sevi için / Dostun evi gönüllerdir, gönüller yapmaya geldim
note: “The Friend” (Dost) is God.

text: Whoever's heart has been brought alive by love *will never die*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 11 (Qazvini-Ghani numbering, as on Ganjoor), couplet beginning “هرگز نمیرد”
original: هرگز نمیرد آن که دلش زنده شد به عشق
note: The couplet goes on: “our permanence is recorded in the ledger of the world”.

text: I follow the religion of love: wherever its camels turn, *love is my religion* and my faith.
author: Ibn Arabi
ref: poem XI, verse 15
original: أدين بدين الحب أنى توجهت ركائبه فالحب ديني وإيماني

text: Knowledge means knowing; knowledge means *knowing yourself*. If you do not know yourself, what is all your reading for?
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “İlim ilim bilmektir”
original: İlim ilim bilmektir, ilim kendin bilmektir / Sen kendini bilmezsin, ya nice okumaktır
note: Manuscripts vary in wording.

text: Brother, *you are your thought*; the rest of you is bone and fiber. If your thought is a rose, you are a rose garden; if a thorn, you are fuel for the furnace.
author: Rumi
ref: Book II, v. 277–278 (Ganjoor II §9, couplets 35–36)
original: ای برادر تو همان اندیشه‌ای / ما بقی تو استخوان و ریشه‌ای / گر گلست اندیشهٔ تو گلشنی / ور بود خاری تو هیمهٔ گلخنی
note: Rumi glossed “thought” here as an inner awareness, not ordinary thinking (Fihi ma fihi, ch. 52).

text: The root of every wrong, every lapse and every craving is being pleased with yourself. The root of every good, every waking and every restraint is *not being pleased with yourself*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 33 at the source (35 in many editions)
original: أصل كل معصية وغفلة وشهوة الرضا عن النفس، وأصل كل طاعة ويقظة وعفة عدم الرضا منك عنها
note: The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: For twelve years I was the blacksmith of my self. I laid it in the furnace of discipline, heated it in the fire of struggle, beat it with the hammer of blame, and *made a mirror of it*.
author: Bayazid Bistami
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Bayazid
original: دوازده سال آهنگر نفس خود بودم، در کوره ریاضت می‌نهادم و با آتش مجاهده می‌تافتم و بر سندان مذمت می‌نهادم و پتک ملامت بر او می‌زدم تا از نفس خویش آینه‌ای کردم
note: Shortened. The saying also has an anvil of reproach, and goes on with five more years of polishing the mirror.

text: *Look kindly at yourself*: you are the essence of the world.
author: Şeyh Galib
ref: refrain couplet of the terci-i bend “Ey dil ey dil niye bu rütbede pür-gamsın sen”
original: Hoşça bak zâtına kim zübde-i âlemsin sen
note: The couplet goes on: “you are the human being who is the pupil of creation’s eye”. Galib was the Mevlevi sheikh of Galata.

text: When your heart tightens, *see the opening inside it*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, Mary and the Holy Spirit (Ganjoor III §179, couplet 40; c. III.3726–3739)
original: چونک قبض آید تو در وی بسط بین
note: The couplet goes on: “stay fresh, and do not knit your brow”. Qabz and bast, tightening and opening, are Sufi terms for the heart’s contraction and expansion.

text: Patience is *swallowing bitterness* without a frown.
author: Junayd of Baghdad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on patience (bab al-sabr)
original: الصبر تجرع المرارة من غير تعبيس
note: His answer when asked what patience is.

text: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan: do not grieve. The house of sorrow will one day be a rose garden: *do not grieve*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 255, opening couplet
original: یوسف گم گشته بازآید به کنعان غم مخور / کلبهٔ احزان شود روزی گلستان غم مخور
note: Jacob grieved for his lost son Joseph in the “house of sorrows” until Joseph came back.

text: God turns ills into good; do not think He does otherwise. The wise only watch: let us see what the Lord will do. *Whatever He does, He does well*.
author: Erzurumlu İbrahim Hakkı
ref: opening stanza (also in his Marifetnâme)
original: Hak şerleri hayr eyler / Zannetme ki gayr eyler / Ârif anı seyr eyler / Mevlâ görelim neyler / Neylerse güzel eyler
note: Tefvîz means handing one’s affairs over to God.

text: I sought a cure for my pain: *my pain was the cure*.
author: Niyazi Mısri
ref: ghazal beginning “Derman arardım derdime”
original: Derman arardım derdime, derdim bana derman imiş
note: Still sung as a hymn (ilahi).

text: A word can end a war; a word can cost a head. A word can turn *poisoned food to honey* and butter.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Keleci bilen kişinin yüzünü ak ede bir söz”
original: Söz ola kese savaşı, söz ola kestire başı / Söz ola ağulu aşı bal ile yağ ede bir söz

text: Until a man speaks, *his faults and gifts* stay hidden.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter I, story 3
original: تا مرد سخن نگفته باشد / عیب و هنرش نهفته باشد

text: Many an Indian and a Turk speak the same tongue; many two Turks are strangers to each other. *Being of one heart* is better than being of one tongue.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the hoopoe and Solomon (Ganjoor I §66, couplets 5–6; c. I.1206–07 in Nicholson)
original: ای بسا هندو و ترک همزبان / ای بسا دو ترک چون بیگانگان / پس زبان محرمی خود دیگرست / همدلی از همزبانی بهترست
note: One half-line between the two is left out: “the language of intimacy is something else”.

text: When talking pleases you, be silent; when silence pleases you, *speak*.
author: Bishr al-Hafi
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on silence (bab al-samt)
original: إذا أعجبك الكلام فاصمت، وإذا أعجبك الصمت فتكلم
note: Bishr “the Barefoot” of Baghdad.

text: Whoever keeps silent about the truth is *a mute devil*.
author: Abu Ali al-Daqqaq
ref: reported by Qushayri (his student), Risala, chapter on silence
original: من سكت عن الحق فهو شيطان أخرس
note: Qushayri heard it from Daqqaq, his teacher.

text: Bury yourself in the earth of obscurity: *unburied seed* never ripens.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 10 at the source (11 in many editions)
original: ادفن وجودك في أرض الخمول، فما نبت مما لم يدفن لا يتم نتاجه
note: Literally: “what grows from what was not buried does not bring its yield to completion”. The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: Wherever there is pain, the cure goes there; wherever there is low ground, water runs. If you want the water of mercy, go, *make yourself low*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book II, v. 1938–1940 (Ganjoor II §40, couplets 7–9)
original: هر کجا دردی دوا آنجا رود / هر کجا پستیست آب آنجا دود / آب رحمت بایدت رو پست شو
note: The couplet goes on: “then drink the wine of mercy and be drunk”.

text: The wise are humble; *the laden branch* bows to the ground.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter IV (on humility), section 2
original: تواضع کند هوشمند گزین / نهد شاخ پرمیوه سر بر زمین

text: To the one who strikes you, *have no hands*; to the one who curses you, have no tongue.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Dervişlik der ki bana, sen derviş olamazsın”
original: Dövene elsiz gerek, sövene dilsiz gerek
note: The couplet goes on: “a dervish must be without self-will, and you cannot be a dervish”.

text: Walk on water and you are a straw; fly through the air and you are a fly. *Win a heart*, and you will be someone.
author: Abdullah Ansari of Herat
ref: third mukhataba (on the ranks of poverty)
original: اگر بر روی آب روی خسی باشی و اگر به هوا پری مگسی باشی، دل به دست آر تا کسی باشی
note: The Persian rhymes: khasī, magasī, kasī. The Mukhatabat is a later compilation of Ansari’s sayings.

text: With every breath the world and we are made new, and we never notice, because it seems to last. Life keeps arriving *fresh, like a stream*, though in the body it looks unbroken.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the cunning of the hare (Ganjoor I §62, couplets 38–39; c. I.1142–43 in Nicholson)
original: هر نفس نو می‌شود دنیا و ما / بی‌خبر از نو شدن اندر بقا / عمر همچون جوی نو نو می‌رسد / مستمری می‌نماید در جسد

text: Until the cloud weeps, *how will the meadow smile*? Until the child cries, how will the milk flow?
author: Rumi
ref: Book V, the guest who soiled the bed (Ganjoor V §5, couplet 17; c. V.133–134)
original: تا نگرید ابر کی خندد چمن / تا نگرید طفل کی جوشد لبن

text: The palace of hope is weakly founded; *life is built on wind*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 37, opening couplet
original: بیا که قصر امل سخت سست بنیادست / بیار باده که بنیاد عمر بر بادست
note: The full line: “Come, the palace of hope is weakly founded; bring wine, for life’s foundation is on the wind.”

text: Son of Adam, you are only days: *each day that goes* takes part of you with it.
author: Hasan al-Basri
ref: reported by Abu Nu'aym al-Isfahani, Hilyat al-Awliya 2:148
original: ابن آدم إنما أنت أيام، كلما ذهب يوم ذهب بعضك
note: Hasan was an early ascetic whom the Sufis count as a forefather.

text: Come, let us be friends and make the work easy. Let us love and be loved: *the world stays with no one*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Hak cihana doludur”
original: Gelin tanış olalım, işi kolay kılalım / Sevelim sevilelim, dünya kimseye kalmaz

text: Look less for water; *get thirst*, so that water springs up for you from above and below.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, v. 3212 (Ganjoor III §151, couplet 9)
original: آب کم جو تشنگی آور به دست / تا بجوشد آبت از بالا و پست

text: Knowledge without action is madness, and *action without knowledge* never happens.
author: al-Ghazali
ref: early in the letter, an “O son” (ayyuha'l-walad) paragraph
original: العلم بلا عمل جنون، والعمل بغير علم لا يكون

text: Hope is what comes with action; otherwise it is *only wishing*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 72 at the source
original: الرجاء ما قارنه عمل، وإلا فهو أمنية
note: The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: Sufism is this: to set down what is in your head, give what is in your hand, and *not flinch* from whatever comes to you.
author: Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr
ref: reported by Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-Tawhid, ch. 2, part 3, sayings no. 13
original: صوفیی چیست؟ گفت: آنچ در سر داری بنهی و آنچ در کف داری بدهی و آنچ بر تو آید نجهی
note: Abu Sa‘id left no writings. His great-great-grandson compiled his sayings about 130 years after his death.

text: You read and write and pile up books on every side: light all around you, *darkness within*, and no knowledge of yourself.
author: Bulleh Shah
ref: kafi “Ilmon bas karin o yaar” (Enough of learning, friend)
note: Bulleh Shah’s kafis came down by word of mouth and in late copies, so the wording varies.

text: The children of Adam are limbs of one another, made of one essence. When one limb aches, the others cannot rest. If you feel nothing at others' pain, you *do not deserve the name human*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter I, story 10
original: بنی آدم اعضای یکدیگرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند / چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار / دگر عضوها را نماند قرار / تو کز محنت دیگران بی‌غمی / نشاید که نامت نهند آدمی
note: Some modern printings read “اعضای یک پیکرند” (limbs of one body).

text: Do not go about hurting anyone, and do as you please: in our law *there is no other sin*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 76 (Ganjoor numbering), couplet beginning “مباش در پی آزار”
original: مباش در پی آزار و هرچه خواهی کن / که در شریعت ما غیر از این گناهی نیست
note: Ghazal numbers differ between editions.

text: If you have *broken a heart even once*, the prayer you pray is no prayer; all seventy-two nations together could not wash your hands and face clean.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Bir kez gönül yıktın ise”
original: Bir kez gönül yıktın ise, bu kıldığın namaz değil / Yetmiş iki millet dahi elin yüzün yumaz değil
note: “Seventy-two nations” means all the peoples and sects of the world.

text: Even if you are hurt, *do not hurt*.
author: Hacı Bektaş Veli
original: İncinsen de incitme
note: A traditional saying of the order, not found in his written works.

text: Wherever you see a broken heart, *be its balm*; when the wronged are stranded on the road, keep them company.
author: Ahmed Yesevi
ref: Hikmet 1, stanza 3
original: Kayda körseng köngli sınuk merhem bolğıl / Andağ mazlum yolda kalsa hemdem bolğıl
note: Middle Turkic. The Divan-i Hikmet survives in late manuscripts and includes poems by his followers.

text: Every breath drawn in sustains life, and every breath let out refreshes the self. So *in each breath are two blessings*, and for each blessing a thanks is owed.
author: Saadi
ref: preface (dibacha), opening lines
original: هر نفسی که فرو می‌رود ممد حیات است و چون بر می‌آید مفرح ذات، پس در هر نفسی دو نعمت موجود است و بر هر نعمتی شکری واجب

text: I never complained of fate but once, when I was barefoot with no money for shoes. Then, in the mosque at Kufa, I saw a man with no feet, and *I gave thanks*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter III (on contentment), story 18 (Ganjoor numbering; 19 in some editions)
original: هرگز از دور زمان ننالیده بودم ... مگر وقتی که پایم برهنه مانده بود و استطاعت پای‌پوشی نداشتم. به جامع کوفه در آمدم دلتنگ، یکی را دیدم که پای نداشت. سپاس نعمت حق به جای آوردم
note: Shortened. The source of the proverb “I cried because I had no shoes, until I met a man who had no feet.”

text: If this market has any profit, *the contented dervish* has it.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 440 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: در این بازار اگر سودی‌ست با درویش خرسند است

text: Pour the sea into a jug and how much will it hold? One day's share. The greedy eye's jug is never full: *until the oyster is content*, it holds no pearl.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, v. 20–21 (Song of the Reed)
original: گر بریزی بحر را در کوزه‌ای / چند گنجد قسمت یک روزه‌ای / کوزهٔ چشم حریصان پر نشد / تا صدف قانع نشد پر در نشد

text: You are free of whatever you have given up hope of, and *a slave to whatever you crave*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 57 at the source
original: أنت حر مما أنت عنه آيس، وعبد لما أنت له طامع
note: The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.
